name: Your First Job: Work Permits, Paychecks and What Bosses Expect
objectives: Given your age and a job offer with a schedule, check whether the job tasks and hours are allowed for your age under federal and state rules, naming the official page you used

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Which jobs and hours are legal at your age
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check whether a job's tasks and hours are allowed for your age.
This lesson builds toward: Given your age and a job offer with a schedule, you will check whether the job tasks and hours are allowed for your age under federal and state rules, naming the official page you used.
In the US, the federal law on child labor is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). States have their own child labor laws too. When the two are different, the stricter rule is the one that applies.
Under federal rules for most non-farm jobs: under 14 you generally cannot work (with a few exceptions on the official page). At 14 and 15 you can work outside school hours, but only up to 3 hours on a school day (Fridays too), 18 hours in a school week, 8 hours on a non-school day and 40 hours in a week with no school, and only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. From June 1 to Labor Day the evening limit moves to 9 p.m.
At 16 and 17, federal law does not limit your hours, but you may not do jobs the Department of Labor calls hazardous. Examples: driving on public roads as part of the job (17-year-olds have a narrow exception), running a forklift or other power-driven hoisting equipment, and most power-driven woodworking machines. Your state may add more limits.
Under 18, if a schedule or task looks against these rules, you are not in trouble: the rules are there to protect you, and the employer is the one who must follow them.
Step by step:
- Write your age and the job's tasks and hours.
- Read the federal rules on the Department of Labor's YouthRules or Fact Sheet 43.
- Open your state's child labor page (the Department of Labor lists every state).
- Use the stricter rule. Circle any hour or task that is not allowed.
Words to know:
- FLSA: the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law on minimum wage, overtime and child labor.
- Child labor law: rules about which jobs and hours are allowed for workers under 18.
- Hazardous job: a task the Department of Labor says is too dangerous for workers under 18, such as driving or running a forklift.
- School week: a week when school is in session for at least one day.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: YouthRules!
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 43, child labor rules for non-farm jobs
- US Department of Labor: State child labor laws
Try it now: A 15-year-old is offered a grocery job on Tuesday and Thursday from 4 to 8 p.m. in October, and Saturday from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. On paper, check each shift against the federal rules. Then open your own state's child labor page and write one rule it adds.
You can now check whether a job's tasks and hours are legal for your age, using federal rules and your state's page.

check.q: You are 15. It is October. Your boss schedules you until 8 p.m. on a school night. What is true under federal rules?
options: It is fine because it is under 3 hours
It is too late: 14- and 15-year-olds stop at 7 p.m. outside summer
It is fine if your parents agree
check.why: Outside June 1 to Labor Day, 14- and 15-year-olds may work only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m.

check.q: Your state's rule is stricter than the federal rule. Which one do you follow?
check.why: When federal and state child labor laws differ, the stricter rule applies.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Work permits and first-day papers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the papers you need to start your job and where to get each one.
This lesson builds toward: For a job in your state, you will list the papers you need to start work and where to get each one, including a work permit if your state requires one, ID for the Form I-9 and the Form W-4.
Federal law does not require a work permit, but many states do for workers under 18. A work permit is sometimes called working papers or an employment certificate. Depending on the state, you may get it from your school, the state labor office or online, and it may need a parent's signature. Check your state's page to see if you need one and how to get it.
On or before your first day, every US employer has you fill in Form I-9. It shows you are allowed to work in the US. You show original ID documents from the list on the form, for example a US passport, or a school ID or state ID together with a Social Security card or birth certificate.
You also fill in Form W-4. It tells your employer how much federal income tax to take out of each paycheck. Your state may have its own tax form too. Ask your boss or a parent if a question confuses you.
Keep it safe: give your Social Security number only on real hiring papers, after you are hired. A real employer never asks you to pay money to get a job or to buy gift cards. That is a scam.
Step by step:
- Check your state's child labor page: do you need a work permit? Who gives it out?
- Find your original ID documents for the Form I-9 (look at the list on the form).
- Read Form W-4 before your first day so you know what it asks.
- Put copies of your papers in one folder. Keep the originals safe at home.
Words to know:
- Work permit: a paper some states require before a person under 18 can work; also called working papers or an employment certificate.
- Form I-9: the federal form that shows you are allowed to work in the US; you show ID documents for it.
- Form W-4: the federal form that tells your employer how much income tax to hold back from your pay.
- Original document: the real paper or card, not a photo or a copy.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 43, child labor rules for non-farm jobs
- US Department of Labor: State child labor laws
- USCIS: Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification
- IRS: About Form W-4
- FTC: Job scams
Try it now: Make a "First Day Papers" checklist on paper. For your state, write: do I need a work permit, and where do I get it? Which two ID documents will I bring for the Form I-9? Who can help me with the Form W-4?
You can now list the papers you need to start a job, where to get each one, and how to keep your private numbers safe.

check.q: Which form shows your employer you are allowed to work in the US?
check.why: Form I-9 checks that you are allowed to work in the US; you show original ID documents for it.

check.q: Someone offers you a job if you first pay $50 for "training materials". What is this most likely?
options: A scam: real employers do not charge you to get a job
A work permit fee from your state
check.why: Asking you to pay to get a job is a common job-scam sign.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: What bosses expect in your first weeks
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the professional action a boss expects in common first-job situations.
This lesson builds toward: Given a workplace situation in your first weeks, you will choose and describe the professional action a boss expects, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
Most first-job bosses care less about experience and more about habits: showing up on time, being ready to work, following instructions, being polite with customers and coworkers, and telling them early when something comes up.
Be on time means ready to work at the start of your shift, not walking in the door. If you are sick or will be late, tell your boss as early as you can, in the way your workplace asks (often a call, not just a text). Do not simply skip a shift.
Keep your phone away while working unless your job allows it. When you do not know how to do something, ask. Repeat back instructions to make sure you understood. Take feedback calmly and say thank you; it means your boss wants you to do well.
Read your schedule every week, and ask for time off early. Being dependable is what gets you more hours, a good reference and your next job.
Step by step:
- Arrive a few minutes early, ready to work.
- If you will be late or sick, tell your boss as early as you can, the way they asked.
- Put your phone away unless the job allows it.
- Ask when you are not sure; repeat back instructions.
- Take feedback calmly and use it.
Words to know:
- Shift: the block of time you are scheduled to work.
- Call out: telling your boss ahead of time that you cannot come to a shift.
- Reference: a person, often a past boss, who tells a new employer what kind of worker you are.
- Feedback: comments on how you are doing and how to do better.
Try it now: Write what you would say in two situations: (1) you wake up sick two hours before your shift; (2) your manager tells you that you stocked a shelf wrong. Say both out loud as if talking to your boss.
You can now choose and describe what a boss expects when you are late or sick, unsure what to do, or getting feedback.

check.q: Your shift starts at 4 p.m. What does "on time" mean?
options: Ready to work at 4:00, so arriving a few minutes early
check.why: On time means ready to start work when the shift begins.

check.q: You are not sure how to use the cash register. What is the best move?
options: Look it up on your phone during the shift
Ask your supervisor to show you, then repeat it back
check.why: Asking and repeating back instructions shows care and prevents mistakes.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Your pay, your rights and your safety

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading your first paystub
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the gross pay, each deduction and the net pay on a paystub.
This lesson builds toward: Given a paystub and your own record of hours, you will find the gross pay, each deduction and the net pay, and check them against your hours, with the math correct to the cent.
A paystub (or pay statement) comes with each paycheck or direct deposit. It shows the pay period, your hours, your pay rate, your gross pay, each deduction and your net pay.
Gross pay is hours times your hourly rate, before anything is taken out. Deductions are amounts taken out. Common ones: federal income tax (based on your Form W-4), Social Security (6.2 percent of your pay) and Medicare (1.45 percent), often shown together as FICA, and in many states a state income tax. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what is left.
Practice only, made-up numbers: 20 hours at $12.00 an hour = $240.00 gross. Social Security: 240 x 0.062 = $14.88. Medicare: 240 x 0.0145 = $3.48. Federal income tax: $6.00. State tax: $3.00. Deductions total $27.36, so net pay = $240.00 - $27.36 = $212.64.
The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. Many states and cities set a higher one, and the higher one applies to you. Check your state's page so you know your rate is legal.
Step by step:
- Find the pay period dates and your hours.
- Check gross pay: hours x rate.
- List each deduction and add them up.
- Check net pay: gross pay minus total deductions.
- If something does not match, ask payroll or your boss politely.
Words to know:
- Gross pay: your pay before anything is taken out: hours x rate.
- Deduction: an amount taken out of your pay, such as taxes.
- Net pay: take-home pay: gross pay minus deductions.
- FICA: the Social Security and Medicare taxes taken from your pay.
- Pay period: the dates of work a paycheck covers.
Official sources:
- IRS: Topic 751, Social Security and Medicare withholding rates
- US Department of Labor: Minimum wage
- US Department of Labor: State minimum wage laws
- IRS: About Form W-4
Try it now: Practice only: you worked 15 hours at $13.00 an hour. Federal income tax is $5.00 and state tax is $2.00. On paper, work out gross pay, Social Security, Medicare, total deductions and net pay. (Answer: $195.00 gross, $12.09, $2.83, $21.92 total, $173.08 net.)
You can now read a paystub, find the gross pay, each deduction and the net pay, and check the math.

check.q: You worked 10 hours at $14.00 an hour. What is your gross pay?
check.why: Gross pay is hours times rate: 10 x $14.00 = $140.00.

check.q: Gross pay is $300.00 and deductions total $35.00. What is net pay?
check.why: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions: $300.00 - $35.00 = $265.00.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Tracking your hours so your pay is right
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep your own record of hours and compare it with your paystub.
This lesson builds toward: Given a paystub and your own record of hours, you will find the gross pay, each deduction and the net pay, and check them against your hours, with the math correct to the cent.
Mistakes happen with pay. The best protection is your own record. Each shift, write the date, the time you started, when your break started and ended, and the time you finished. The Department of Labor has a free timesheet app, or you can use a notebook or your phone's notes.
Add up the hours for the pay period. Remember to take out unpaid meal breaks. Then compare your total with the hours on your paystub.
If the numbers do not match, do not panic and do not accuse. Bring your record to your boss or payroll and ask: "My notes show 22 hours, and my paystub shows 19. Can you help me check?" Most mistakes are fixed this way.
If you are not paid for hours you worked and it is not fixed, the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division takes complaints. It is free and confidential.
Step by step:
- Each shift: write the date, start time, break times and end time.
- At the end of the pay period, add up your hours (minus unpaid breaks).
- Compare your total with the hours on your paystub.
- If they differ, bring your record and ask politely to check.
- If it is not fixed, contact the Wage and Hour Division.
Words to know:
- Timesheet: a record of the days and hours you worked.
- Unpaid break: a meal break when you are fully off duty and not paid.
- Payroll: the person or team that pays workers.
- Wage and Hour Division: the part of the US Department of Labor that enforces pay and child labor rules.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: YouthRules!
- US Department of Labor: Child labor
Try it now: Practice only: Monday 3:30 to 7:00 p.m., Wednesday 3:30 to 7:00 p.m., Saturday 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. with a 30-minute unpaid lunch. Add up the hours. Your paystub says 11 hours. Write what you would say to your boss. (Answer: 3.5 + 3.5 + 5.5 = 12.5 hours.)
You can now keep a record of your hours, compare it with your paystub, and ask politely to fix a mistake.

check.q: You worked 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. with a 30-minute unpaid lunch. How many paid hours?
check.why: 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. is 5 hours; minus a 30-minute unpaid break is 4.5 hours.

check.q: Your notes show 22 hours, but your paystub shows 19. What do you do first?
options: Bring your record to your boss or payroll and ask politely to check
check.why: Most pay mistakes are fixed by showing your record and asking politely.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your rights and safety: speaking up
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Describe the steps to speak up and report an unsafe or unfair situation.
This lesson builds toward: Given an unsafe or unfair situation at work, you will describe the steps to speak up and report it, naming who you tell first and the official agency to call if it is not fixed.
Every worker, including teens, has rights. Your employer must give you a safe workplace and pay you at least the legal minimum wage for every hour you work. You should get training before you do a task, and you can ask questions. Your employer cannot punish you for asking about your rights or for making a complaint.
Young workers get hurt more often when they are new, rushed or untrained. Warning signs: being told to use a machine you were not trained on, a task that is banned for your age, no protective gear, slippery floors, hot oil, or being left alone late at night.
Steps to speak up: stop if you are in danger. Tell your supervisor calmly what the problem is. If they do not fix it, tell another manager and a parent, teacher or job-program staff. If it is still not fixed, contact the government: OSHA (1-800-321-6742) for safety, or the Wage and Hour Division (1-866-487-9243) for pay, hours or child labor problems.
If someone is badly hurt, call 911 (or your local emergency number) first.
Step by step:
- If you are in danger, stop and move away.
- Tell your supervisor calmly what is wrong.
- If it is not fixed, tell another manager and a trusted adult.
- Still not fixed: call OSHA for safety or the Wage and Hour Division for pay, hours or child labor.
- Emergency: call 911 first.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency for workplace safety.
- Retaliation: punishing a worker for speaking up or making a complaint; it is not allowed.
- Protective gear: items like gloves, goggles or non-slip shoes that keep you safe.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Young workers
- US Department of Labor: YouthRules!
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 43, child labor rules for non-farm jobs
Try it now: You are 16. Your manager tells you to use the meat slicer at a deli, and you have had no training. Write the words you would say to your manager, and who you would tell next if they insist. Save the OSHA and Wage and Hour numbers in your phone.
You can now spot an unsafe or unfair situation and speak up in steps: your supervisor, a trusted adult, then the official agency.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Hours and tasks checked No age rules written, or a shift or task that breaks the rules is not noticed. Each shift and task is checked against federal and state rules, with the official page named. Also notes a state rule that is stricter than the federal rule and how it changes the schedule. Papers ready The checklist is missing the Form I-9, Form W-4 or the state work permit question. Lists the work permit (if needed), ID for the Form I-9 and Form W-4, and where to get each. Also lists how to keep private numbers safe and one job-scam sign. Paystub checked Gross pay, deductions or net pay are missing or the math is wrong. Gross pay, each deduction and net pay are written and the math is right to the cent. Also compares the paystub hours with a written timesheet and says what to do if they differ. Boss expectations Habits are vague, like "be good". Three clear habits, such as arriving early, calling out early and asking when unsure. Each habit has a short script of what the learner would say. Safety plan No plan, or the plan skips telling a supervisor or naming an agency. Names who to tell first, a trusted adult, and OSHA or the Wage and Hour Division with the phone number. Also says to call 911 first in an emergency and lists warning signs for the learner's own job. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Your boss tells you to clean a fryer with hot oil and gives you no gloves or training. What do you do first?
options: Tell your supervisor calmly that you need training and gear before you do it
Do it fast so you do not get in trouble
check.why: Speaking up to your supervisor first is the usual first step when no one is hurt yet.

check.q: You told two managers about a pay problem and nothing changed. Who can you contact?
options: The US Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division
check.why: The Wage and Hour Division takes free, confidential complaints about pay, hours and child labor.
